{{Short description|Theorem in combinatorics on words}}
{{distinguish|Cobham's thesis}}
'''Cobham's theorem''' is a theorem in [[combinatorics on words]] that has important connections with [[number theory]], notably [[transcendental numbers]], and [[automata theory]]. Informally, the theorem gives the condition for the members of a set ''S'' of natural numbers written in [[Radix|bases]] ''b<sub>1</sub>'' and base ''b<sub>2</sub>'' to be recognised by [[Finite automaton|finite automata]]. Specifically, consider bases ''b<sub>1</sub>'' and ''b<sub>2</sub>'' such that they are not powers of the same [[integer]]. Cobham's theorem states that ''S'' written in bases ''b<sub>1</sub>'' and ''b<sub>2</sub>'' is recognised by finite automata if and only if ''S'' differs by a [[finite set]] from a finite union of [[arithmetic progression]]s. The theorem was proved by [[Alan Cobham (mathematician)|Alan Cobham]] in 1969<ref name=Cobham>{{Cite journal|last=Cobham|first=Alan|year=1969|title=On the base-dependence of sets of numbers recognizable by finite automata|journal=Mathematical Systems Theory|volume=3|issue=2|pages=186–192 |doi=10.1007/BF01746527|doi-access=free|mr=0250789}}</ref> and has since given rise to many extensions and generalisations.<ref>{{Cite book|first1=Fabien|first2=Michel|last1=Durand|last2=Rigo|title=Automata: from Mathematics to Applications|publisher=European Mathematical Society|year=2010|orig-date=Chapter originally written 2010|chapter=On Cobham’s Theorem|editor-last=Pin|editor-first=J.-É.|chapter-url=https://www-fourier.ujf-grenoble.fr/sites/default/files/files/fichiers/cobham010711.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|first1=Boris|first2=Jason|last1=Adamczewski|last2=Bell|title=Automata: from Mathematics to Applications|publisher=European Mathematical Society|year=2010|orig-date=Chapter originally written 2010|chapter=Automata in number theory|editor-last=Pin|editor-first=J.-É.|chapter-url=https://adamczewski.perso.math.cnrs.fr/Chapter25.pdf}}</ref>

== Definitions ==
Let <math>n>0</math> be an integer. The representation of a natural number <math display="inline">n</math> in [[Radix|base]] <math display="inline">b</math> is the sequence of digits <math>n_0n_1\cdots n_h</math> such that

: <math>n=n_0+n_1b+\cdots+n_hb^h</math>

where <math>0\le n_0,n_1,\ldots,n_h < b</math> and <math>n_h>0</math>. The word <math>n_0n_1\cdots n_h</math> is often denoted <math>\langle n\rangle_b</math>, or more simply, <math>n_b</math>.

A set of natural numbers ''S'' is ''recognisable in base'' <math display="inline">b</math> or more simply [[Automatic sequence|''<math display="inline">b</math>-recognisable'']] or ''<math display="inline">b</math>-automatic'' if the set <math>\{n_b\mid n\in S\}</math> of the representations of its elements in base <math>b</math> is a language recognisable by a [[Deterministic finite automaton|finite automaton]] on the alphabet <math>\{0,1,\ldots,b-1\}</math>.

Two positive integers <math>k</math> and <math>\ell</math> are [[Multiplicative independence|multiplicatively independent]] if there are no non-negative integers <math>p</math> and <math>q</math> such that <math>k^p=\ell^q</math>. For example, 2 and 3 are multiplicatively independent, but 8 and 16 are not since <math>8^4=16^3</math>. Two integers are multiplicatively dependent [[if and only if]] they are powers of a same third integer.

== Problem statements ==

=== Original problem statement ===
More equivalent statements of the theorem have been given. The original version by Cobham is the following:<ref name=Cobham/> {{Math theorem|Let <math>S</math> be a set of non-negative integers and let <math>m</math> and <math>n</math> be multiplicatively independent positive integers. Then <math>S</math> is recognizable by finite automata in both <math>m</math>-ary and <math>n</math>-ary notation if and only if it is ultimately periodic.
| name = Theorem (Cobham 1969)
}}Another way to state the theorem is by using [[automatic sequence]]s. Cobham himself calls them "uniform tag sequences."<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Cobham|first=Alan|year=1972|title=Uniform tag sequences|journal=Mathematical Systems Theory|volume=6|issue=1–2|pages=164–192 |doi=10.1007/BF01706087|doi-access=free|mr=0457011}}</ref> The following form is found in Allouche and Shallit's book:<ref name="as345">{{Cite book|last1=Allouche|first1=Jean-Paul|author-link1=:fr:Jean-Paul Allouche|title=Automatic Sequences: theory, applications, generalizations|last2=Shallit|first2=Jeffrey|author-link2=Jeffrey Shallit|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|year=2003|isbn=0-521-82332-3|location=Cambridge|page=350}}</ref>{{Math theorem|Theorem|Let <math>k</math> and <math>\ell</math> be two multiplicatively independent integers. A sequence is both <math>k</math>-automatic and <math>\ell</math>-automatic only if it is <math>1</math>-automatic<ref>A "1-automatic" sequence is a sequence that is ultimately periodic</ref>
}}We can show that the characteristic sequence of a set of natural numbers ''S'' recognisable by finite automata in base ''k'' is a ''k''-automatic sequence and that conversely, for all ''k''-automatic sequences <math>u</math> and all integers <math>0\le i <k</math>, the set <math>S_i</math> of natural numbers <math>s</math> such that <math>u_s=i</math> is recognisable in base <math>k</math>.

=== Formulation in logic ===
Cobham's theorem can be formulated in [[first-order logic]] using a theorem proven by Büchi in 1960.<ref>{{cite book | first=J. R. | last=Büchi | chapter=Weak Second-Order Arithmetic and Finite Automata | date=1990 | title=The Collected Works of J. Richard Büchi | series=Z. Math. Logik Grundlagen Math. | volume=6 | page=87 | doi=10.1007/978-1-4613-8928-6_22 | isbn=978-1-4613-8930-9 }}</ref> This formulation in logic allows for extensions and generalisations. The logical expression uses the theory<ref name="VB">{{Cite web|last1=Bruyère|first1=Véronique|author1-link=Véronique Bruyère|year=2010|title=Around Cobham's theorem and some of its extensions|url=http://www.mat.uc.pt/~amgc/daast/slides/daast-bruyere|access-date=19 January 2017|website=Dynamical Aspects of Automata and Semigroup Theories|publisher=Satellite Workshop of Highlights of AutoMathA}}</ref>

: <math>\langle N, +, V_r\rangle</math>

of natural integers equipped with addition and the function <math>V_r</math> defined by <math>V_r(0)=1</math> and for any positive integer <math display="inline">n</math>, <math>V_r(n)=r^m</math> if <math>r^m</math> is the largest power of <math>r</math> that divides <math display="inline">n</math>. For example, <math>V_2(20)=4</math>, and <math>V_3(20)=1</math>.

A set of integers <math>S</math> is ''definable in first-order logic in'' <math>\langle N, +, V_r\rangle</math> if it can be described by a first-order formula with equality, addition, and <math>V_r</math>.

Examples:

* The set of odd numbers is definable (without <math>V_r</math>) by the formula <math>(\exists y)(x=y+y+1)</math>
* The set <math>\{2^n\mid n\ge0\}</math> of the powers of 2 is definable by the simple formula <math>V_2(x)=x</math>.
{{Math theorem|Let ''S'' be a set of natural numbers, and let <math>k</math> and <math>\ell</math> be two multiplicatively independent positive integers. Then ''S'' is first-order definable in
<math>\langle N, +, V_k\rangle</math> and in <math>\langle N, +, V_\ell\rangle</math> if and only if ''S'' is ultimately periodic.
| name = Cobham's theorem reformulated
}}We can push the analogy with logic further by noting that ''S'' is first-order definable in [[Presburger arithmetic]] if and only if it is ultimately periodic. So, a set ''S'' is definable in the logics <math>\langle N, +, V_k\rangle</math> and <math>\langle N, +, V_\ell\rangle</math> if and only if it is definable in [[Presburger arithmetic]].

== Generalisations ==

=== Approach by morphisms ===
An automatic sequence is a particular [[morphic word]], whose [[Morphic word|morphism]] is [[Free monoid#Morphisms|uniform]], meaning that the length of the images generated by the morphism for each letter of its input alphabet is the same. A set of integers is hence ''k''-recognisable if and only if its characteristic sequence is generated by a uniform morphism followed by a [[Morphic word|coding]], where a coding is a morphism that maps each letter of the input alphabet to a letter of the output alphabet. For example, the [[Indicator function|characteristic sequence]] of the powers of 2 is produced by the 2-uniform morphism (meaning each letter is mapped to a word of length 2) over the alphabet <math>B=\{a,0,1\}</math> defined by

: <math>a \mapsto a1\ ,\quad 1\mapsto 10\ ,\quad 0\mapsto 00</math>

which generates the infinite word

: <math>a11010001\cdots</math>,

followed by the coding (that is, letter to letter) that maps <math>a</math> to <math>0</math> and leaves <math>0</math> and <math>1</math> unchanged, giving

: <math>011010001\cdots</math>.

The notion has been extended as follows:<ref name=Dur2011>{{Cite journal|last=Durand|first=Fabien|year=2011|title=Cobham's theorem for substitutions|url=http://www.ems-ph.org/journals/show_pdf.php?issn=1435-9855&vol=13&iss=6&rank=8|journal=[[Journal of the European Mathematical Society]]|volume=13|issue=6|pages=1797–1812|arxiv=1010.4009|doi=10.4171/JEMS/294|doi-access=free}}</ref> a morphic word <math>s</math> is <math>\alpha</math>-''substitutive'' for a certain number <math>\alpha</math> if when written in the form

: <math>s=\pi(f^\omega(b))</math>

where the morphism <math>f:B^*\to B^*</math>, [[Morphic word|prolongable]] in <math display="inline">b</math>, has the following properties:

* all letters of <math>B</math> occur in <math>f^\omega(b)</math>, and
* <math>\alpha>1</math> is the dominant [[eigenvalue]] of the [[Morphic word|matrix of morphism]] <math>f</math>, namely, the matrix <math>M(f)=(m_{x,y})_{x\in B,y\in A}</math>, where <math>m_{x,y}</math> is the number of occurrences of the letter <math>x</math> in the word <math>f(y)</math>.

A set ''S'' of natural numbers is <math>\alpha</math>-''recognisable'' if its characteristic sequence <math>s</math> is <math>\alpha</math>-substitutive.

A last definition: a ''[[Perron number]]'' is an [[algebraic number]] <math>z > 1</math> such that all its conjugates belong to the disc <math>\{z' \in \Complex,|z'|< z\}</math>. These are exactly the dominant eigenvalues of the primitive matrices of positive integers.

We then have the following statement:<ref name=Dur2011/>{{Math theorem|Let ''α'' et ''β'' be two multiplicatively independent Perron numbers. Then a sequence ''x'' with elements belonging to a finite set is both ''α''-substitutive and ''β''-substitutive if and only if ''x'' is ultimately periodic.
| name = Cobham's theorem for substitutions
}}

=== Logic approach ===
The logic equivalent permits to consider more general situations: the automatic sequences over the natural numbers <math>\N</math> or recognisable sets have been extended to the integers <math>\Z</math>, to the Cartesian products <math>\N^m</math>, to the real numbers <math>\R</math> and to the Cartesian products <math>\R^m</math>.<ref name="VB" />

; Extension to <math>\Z</math>

We code the base <math>k</math> integers by prepending to the representation of a positive integer the digit <math>0</math>, and by representing negative integers by <math>k-1</math> followed by the number's [[Method of complements|<math>k</math>-complement]]. For example, in base 2, the integer <math>-6=-8+2</math> is represented as <math>1010</math>. The powers of 2 are written as <math>010^*</math>, and their negatives <math>110^*</math> (since <math>11000</math> is the representation of <math>-16+8=-8</math>).

; Extension to <math>\N^m</math>

A subset <math>X</math> of <math>N^m</math> is recognisable in base <math>k</math> if the elements of <math>X</math>, written as vectors with <math>m</math> components, are recognisable over the resulting alphabet.

For example, in base 2, we have <math>3=11_2</math> and <math>9=1001_2</math>; the vector  <math>\begin{pmatrix}3\\9\end{pmatrix}</math> is written as <math>\begin{pmatrix}0011\\1001\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\1\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}0\\0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix}</math>.{{Math theorem|Let <math>r</math> and <math>s</math> be two multiplicatively independent positive integers. A subset <math>S</math> of <math>N^m</math> is <math>r</math>-recognisable and <math>s</math>-recognisable if and only if <math>S</math> is describable in Presburger arithmetic.
| name = Semenov's theorem (1977)<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Semenov|first=Alexei Lvovich|year=1977|title=Predicates regular in two number systems are Presburger|journal=Sib. Mat. Zh.|language=ru|volume=18|pages=403–418|doi=10.1007/BF00967164 |mr=0450050|zbl=0369.02023|s2cid=119658350 }}</ref>
}}An elegant proof of this theorem is given by Muchnik in 1991 by induction on <math>m</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Muchnik|journal=Theoretical Computer Science|title=The definable criterion for definability in Presburger arithmetic and its applications|year=2003|url=https://core.ac.uk/download/pdf/82333239.pdf|doi=10.1016/S0304-3975(02)00047-6|volume=290|issue=3|pages=1433–1444 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Other extensions have been given to the real numbers and vectors of real numbers.<ref name="VB" />

== Proofs ==
[[Samuel Eilenberg]] announced the theorem without proof in his book;<ref>{{Cite book|last=Eilenberg|first=Samuel|title=Automata, Languages and Machines, Vol. A|publisher=[[Academic Press]]|year=1974|isbn=978-0-12-234001-7|series=Pure and Applied Mathematics|location=New York|pages=xvi+451|issue=58}}.
</ref> he says "The proof is correct, long, and hard. It is a challenge to find a more reasonable proof of this fine theorem." Georges Hansel proposed a more simple proof, published in the not-easily accessible proceedings of a conference.<ref>{{Cite book|title=Actes de la Fête des mots|place=Rouen|publisher=Greco de programmation, CNRS|year=1982|pages=55–59|last1=Hansel|first1=Georges|language=fr|chapter=À propos d'un théorème de Cobham|editor-last=Perrin|editor-first=D.}}</ref> The proof of Dominique Perrin<ref>{{Cite book|first1=Dominique|last1=Perrin|editor-last=van Leeuwen|editor-first=Jan|title=Handbook of Theoretical Computer Science|volume=B: Formal Models and Semantics|publisher=Elsevier|year=1990|isbn=978-0444880741|chapter=Finite Automata|pages=1–57}}</ref> and that of Allouche and Shallit's book<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Allouche|first1=Jean-Paul|author-link1=:fr:Jean-Paul Allouche|title=Automatic Sequences: theory, applications, generalizations|last2=Shallit|first2=Jeffrey|author-link2=Jeffrey Shallit|publisher=[[Cambridge University Press]]|year=2003|isbn=0-521-82332-3|location=Cambridge}}</ref> contain the same error in one of the lemmas, mentioned in the list of errata of the book.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/~shallit/as-errata.pdf |title=Errata for Automatic Sequences: Theory, Applications, Generalizations |last1=Shallit |first1=Jeffrey |last2=Allouche |first2=Jean-Paul |date=31 March 2020 |access-date=25 June 2021}}</ref> This error was uncovered in a note by Tomi Kärki,<ref>{{Cite web|last=Tomi Kärki|year=2005|title=A Note on the Proof of Cobham's Theorem|url=http://www.tucs.fi/publications/attachment.php?fname=TR713.pdf|access-date=23 January 2017|website=Rapport Technique n° 713|publisher=University of Turku}}</ref> and corrected by Michel Rigo and Laurent Waxweiler.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Michel Rigo|last2=Laurent Waxweiler|year=2006|title=A Note on Syndeticity, Recognizable Sets and Cobham's Theorem.|url=http://eatcs.org/images/bulletin/beatcs88.pdf|journal=Bulletin of the EATCS|volume=88|pages=169–173 |arxiv=0907.0624|mr=2222340|zbl=1169.68490|access-date=23 January 2017}}</ref> This part of the proof has been recently written.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Paul Fermé, Willy Quach and Yassine Hamoudi|year=2015|title=Le théorème de Cobham|language=French |trans-title=Cobham's Theorem|url=http://perso.ens-lyon.fr/yassine.hamoudi/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/Cobham.pdf|access-date=24 January 2017|archive-date=2017-02-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170202033005/http://perso.ens-lyon.fr/yassine.hamoudi/wp-content/uploads/2016/07/Cobham.pdf}}</ref>

In January 2018, Thijmen J. P. Krebs announced, on [[ArXiv|Arxiv]], a simplified proof of the original theorem, based on [[Dirichlet's approximation theorem|Dirichlet's approximation criterion]] instead of that of Kronecker; the article appeared in 2021.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Krebs|first=Thijmen J. P.|year=2021|title=A More Reasonable Proof of Cobham's Theorem|journal=International Journal of Foundations of Computer Science|volume=32|issue=2|page=203207|arxiv=1801.06704|doi=10.1142/S0129054121500118|s2cid=39850911 |issn=0129-0541}}</ref> The employed method has been refined and used by Mol, Rampersad, Shallit and Stipulanti.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Mol|first1=Lucas|last2=Rampersad|first2=Narad|last3=Shallit|first3=Jeffrey|last4=Stipulanti|first4=Manon|year=2019|title=Cobham's Theorem and Automaticity|journal=International Journal of Foundations of Computer Science|volume=30|issue=8|pages=1363–1379|arxiv=1809.00679|doi=10.1142/S0129054119500308|s2cid=52156852 |issn=0129-0541}}</ref>
